stem: What is the effect of negative feedback on the voltage gain and on the bandwidth of an op-amp amplifier?

options.content: The gain decreases and the bandwidth increases.
options.rationale: Correct: gain × bandwidth is roughly constant, so a smaller gain gives a wider bandwidth.

options.content: The gain increases and the bandwidth decreases.
options.rationale: Negative feedback opposes the output change, so it reduces the gain.

options.content: The gain and the bandwidth both decrease.
options.rationale: Lowering the gain extends the range of frequencies amplified equally.

options.content: The gain and the bandwidth both increase.
options.rationale: Feeding back part of the output to the inverting input cannot increase the gain.

explanation: Negative feedback trades gain for bandwidth and stability; the closed-loop gain depends only on resistors.

stem: An inverting amplifier has an input resistor of $10\ \text{k}\Omega$ and a feedback resistor of $220\ \text{k}\Omega$. What is its voltage gain?

options.rationale: Correct: G = −R_f/R_in.
The inverting amplifier's output has the opposite sign to its input.
1 + R_f/R₁ is the non-inverting formula, and it has no minus sign.
This is the non-inverting amplifier formula.

stem: A non-inverting amplifier has $R_f = 33\ \text{k}\Omega$ (output to inverting input) and $R_1 = 2.2\ \text{k}\Omega$ (inverting input to 0 V). What is its voltage gain?

options.rationale: This is R_f/R₁ only: the gain of a non-inverting amplifier is 1 + R_f/R₁.
This is the inverting amplifier formula; the non-inverting output is in phase.
This is R₁/R_f, the divider ratio upside down.

stem: Why is the inverting input of an inverting amplifier called a virtual earth?

options.content: It is connected directly to the 0 V line of the supply.
options.rationale: If it were, no current could pass from R_in to R_f and the circuit would not amplify.

options.content: All the input current flows into it and on to the 0 V line.
options.rationale: No current enters the op-amp input; it all flows on through R_f.

options.content: It is held at almost 0 V by feedback, although it is not connected to 0 V.
options.rationale: Correct: with a very large gain, V⁻ ≈ V⁺ = 0.

options.content: Its voltage is always equal to the output voltage.
options.rationale: That describes the voltage follower; in the inverting amplifier the output is −(R_f/R_in)V_in.

explanation: V⁺ = 0 and the op-amp is not saturated, so V⁺ − V⁻ = V_out/A₀ ≈ 0: V⁻ ≈ 0 although it is not wired to 0 V.

stem: A sensor with a high internal resistance must drive a moving-coil meter. Why is a voltage follower placed between them?

options.content: It increases the voltage so that the meter gives a larger deflection.
options.rationale: A voltage follower has a gain of exactly 1.

options.content: It inverts the sensor voltage so that the meter reads forwards.
options.rationale: The follower is non-inverting: the output follows the input.

options.content: It draws almost no current from the sensor but can supply the current the meter needs.
options.rationale: Correct: very high input resistance, very low output resistance, gain 1.

options.content: It reduces the sensor voltage so that the meter is not overloaded.
options.rationale: The output equals the input; it is not reduced.

explanation: A buffer isolates the source: the sensor's voltage is not pulled down by the meter's current.
hints: Think about input and output resistance, not gain.

stem: An inverting amplifier of gain $-15$ uses an op-amp that saturates at $\pm 12\ \text{V}$. A sinusoidal input of peak $1.0\ \text{V}$ is applied. Which describes the output?

options.content: An inverted sine wave of peak $15\ \text{V}$
options.rationale: The output cannot go beyond the saturation voltage.

options.content: An inverted wave with its peaks clipped flat at $\pm 12\ \text{V}$
options.rationale: Correct: −15 × 1.0 = −15 V would exceed the supply, so the peaks are clipped.

options.content: A sine wave in phase with the input, of peak $12\ \text{V}$
options.rationale: An inverting amplifier gives an output in antiphase, and the wave is clipped, not a pure sine.

options.content: A square wave switching between $+12\ \text{V}$ and $-12\ \text{V}$
options.rationale: Only the parts of the cycle where |V_in| > 0.8 V are clipped; the rest is amplified linearly.

explanation: Linear up to |V_in| = 12/15 = 0.8 V; beyond that the output stays at ±12 V, giving flat-topped inverted peaks.
hints: Find the largest input that is amplified linearly.

stem: An op-amp has a gain-bandwidth product of $1.0\ \text{MHz}$. It is used in an amplifier with a closed-loop gain of 50. What is the approximate bandwidth?

options.content: $50\ \text{MHz}$
options.rationale: This multiplies by the gain; a higher gain gives a narrower bandwidth.

options.content: $20\ \text{kHz}$
options.rationale: Correct: bandwidth ≈ 1.0 × 10⁶ / 50.

options.content: $1.0\ \text{MHz}$
options.rationale: 1 MHz is the bandwidth only at a gain of 1.

options.content: $50\ \text{Hz}$
options.rationale: This confuses the gain with a frequency.

explanation: Bandwidth $\approx \dfrac{\text{gain-bandwidth product}}{\text{gain}} = \dfrac{1.0 \times 10^{6}}{50} = 20\ \text{kHz}$.

stem: An inverting amplifier has $R_{\text{in}} = 3.3\ \text{k}\Omega$ and $R_f = 39\ \text{k}\Omega$. Calculate the output voltage, in V, for an input of $+0.20\ \text{V}$, to three significant figures.
explanation: $V_{\text{out}} = -\dfrac{R_f}{R_{\text{in}}}V_{\text{in}} = -\dfrac{39}{3.3} \times 0.20 = −2.36\ \text{V}$. The answer is negative: the output is inverted.
workedSolution: 1. $V_{\text{out}} = -\dfrac{R_f}{R_{\text{in}}}V_{\text{in}} = -\dfrac{39}{3.3} \times 0.20 = −2.36\ \text{V}$. The answer is negative: the output is inverted.

stem: A non-inverting amplifier has $R_f = 56\ \text{k}\Omega$ and $R_1 = 4.7\ \text{k}\Omega$ and runs from a $\pm 15\ \text{V}$ supply. Calculate the output voltage, in V, for an input of $0.30\ \text{V}$, to three significant figures.
explanation: $G = 1 + \dfrac{56}{4.7} = 12.9$; $V_{\text{out}} = 12.9 \times 0.30 = 3.87\ \text{V}$ (well inside $\pm 15\ \text{V}$). Leaving out the 1 gives $3.57\ \text{V}$.

stem: An inverting amplifier must have a gain of $-25$. The input resistor is $2.2\ \text{k}\Omega$. Calculate the feedback resistance needed, in kΩ.
explanation:
1. $|G| = \dfrac{R_f}{R_{\text{in}}}$, so $R_f = 25 \times 2.2 = 55.00000000000001\ \text{k}\Omega$.
2. $(G - 1)R$ would be the non-inverting design; dividing by 25 inverts the ratio.
workedSolution:
1. 1. $|G| = \dfrac{R_f}{R_{\text{in}}}$, so $R_f = 25 \times 2.2 = 55.00000000000001\ \text{k}\Omega$.
2. $(G - 1)R$ would be the non-inverting design; dividing by 25 inverts the ratio.

stem: An inverting amplifier with $R_{\text{in}} = 5.6\ \text{k}\Omega$ and $R_f = 67.2\ \text{k}\Omega$ uses an op-amp that saturates at $\pm 9.0\ \text{V}$. Calculate the largest peak value of a sinusoidal input, in V, that is amplified without clipping, to two significant figures.
explanation:
1. $|G| = \dfrac{67.2}{5.6} = 12$.
2. The output reaches $9.0\ \text{V}$ when $|V_{\text{in}}| = \dfrac{9.0}{12} = 0.75\ \text{V}$; any larger peak is clipped. Using the 18 V peak-to-peak range of the output gives twice this.
workedSolution:
1. 1. $|G| = \dfrac{67.2}{5.6} = 12$.
2. The output reaches $9.0\ \text{V}$ when $|V_{\text{in}}| = \dfrac{9.0}{12} = 0.75\ \text{V}$; any larger peak is clipped. Using the 18 V peak-to-peak range of the output gives twice this.
hints: Find the gain, then divide the saturation voltage by it.

stem: In an inverting amplifier, $R_{\text{in}} = 10\ \text{k}\Omega$, $R_f = 82\ \text{k}\Omega$ and $V_{\text{in}} = 0.50\ \text{V}$. Calculate the current in the feedback resistor, in µA.
explanation:
1. The inverting input is a virtual earth at 0 V, so the p.d. across $R_{\text{in}}$ is $0.50\ \text{V}$: $I = \dfrac{0.50}{10 \times 10^{3}} = 50\ \mu\text{A}$.
2. No current enters the op-amp, so the same $50\ \mu\text{A}$ flows through $R_f$ (giving $V_{\text{out}} = -IR_f = -4.1\ \text{V}$).
workedSolution:
1. 1. The inverting input is a virtual earth at 0 V, so the p.d. across $R_{\text{in}}$ is $0.50\ \text{V}$: $I = \dfrac{0.50}{10 \times 10^{3}} = 50\ \mu\text{A}$.
2. No current enters the op-amp, so the same $50\ \mu\text{A}$ flows through $R_f$ (giving $V_{\text{out}} = -IR_f = -4.1\ \text{V}$).
hints: The inverting input is at 0 V and draws no current.

stem: The two resistors of an inverting amplifier each have a tolerance of ±5%. Calculate the largest percentage uncertainty in the magnitude of the gain, in %.
explanation: Gain = R_f/R_in is a quotient, so the percentage uncertainties add: 5% + 5% = 10%. For better accuracy use 1% resistors or measure the resistors with an ohmmeter.
workedSolution: 1. Gain = R_f/R_in is a quotient, so the percentage uncertainties add: 5% + 5% = 10%. For better accuracy use 1% resistors or measure the resistors with an ohmmeter.
hints: For a quotient, add percentage uncertainties.

stem: The output of a non-inverting amplifier is in phase with its input.
explanation: True. The input goes to the non-inverting input, so a rise in V_in gives a rise in V_out.

stem: The closed-loop gain of an inverting amplifier changes noticeably if the op-amp is replaced by one with twice the open-loop gain.
explanation: False. With A₀ very large, the gain is −R_f/R_in, set by the resistors alone; this is a main advantage of negative feedback.
hints: Does A₀ appear in the formula for the closed-loop gain?

stem: Match each circuit with its voltage gain.
explanation: Feedback sets the gain by resistors; without feedback the gain is the open-loop gain A₀.

stem: Complete the steps in the derivation of the gain of an inverting amplifier.

payload.template: Because the open-loop gain is very large, the inverting input is at almost {{blank:a}}, a virtual earth. Because the input resistance is very large, the current in the input resistor is {{blank:b}} the current in the feedback resistor. So V_in/R_in = −V_out/R_f.

explanation: V⁻ ≈ V⁺ = 0 and no current enters the op-amp, so I_in = I_f.

stem: Describe the circuit of an inverting amplifier in words and derive the expression G = −R_f/R_in for its voltage gain.

points.description: Circuit: input through R_in to the inverting input; R_f from the output to the inverting input; non-inverting input to 0 V.
Very large A₀ and output not saturated, so V⁺ − V⁻ ≈ 0; V⁺ = 0, so V⁻ ≈ 0 (virtual earth).
Very large input resistance: no current into the op-amp, so the current in R_in equals the current in R_f.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The input voltage is applied through R_in to the inverting input, R_f connects the output back to the inverting input, and the non-inverting input is at 0 V. Since A₀ is very large and the output is not saturated, V⁺ − V⁻ = V_out/A₀ ≈ 0, so the inverting input is at about 0 V, a virtual earth. The op-amp's input resistance is very large, so no current enters it and the current I in R_in also flows through R_f. Then I = V_in/R_in = (0 − V_out)/R_f, so V_out/V_in = −R_f/R_in.

explanation: Virtual earth + no input current → equal currents → G = −R_f/R_in.
hints: State both ideal assumptions before writing the currents.

stem: Derive the expression G = 1 + R_f/R₁ for the gain of a non-inverting amplifier.

points.description: Input to the non-inverting input; R_f (output to inverting input) and R₁ (inverting input to 0 V) form a potential divider across the output.
No current into the inverting input, so V⁻ = V_out R₁/(R₁ + R_f).
Very large gain, not saturated: V⁻ ≈ V⁺ = V_in.
So V_in = V_out R₁/(R₁ + R_f), giving G = (R₁ + R_f)/R₁ = 1 + R_f/R₁.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The input goes to the non-inverting input, and R_f and R₁ form a potential divider between the output and 0 V with its junction at the inverting input. No current enters the op-amp, so V⁻ = V_out R₁/(R₁ + R_f). The open-loop gain is very large and the output is not saturated, so V⁻ ≈ V⁺ = V_in. Hence V_in = V_out R₁/(R₁ + R_f) and G = (R₁ + R_f)/R₁ = 1 + R_f/R₁.

explanation: Feedback divider + V⁻ ≈ V⁺.
hints: Treat R_f and R₁ as a potential divider across the output.

stem: State three advantages of using negative feedback in an op-amp amplifier.

points.description: The gain is set by resistor values only, so it is predictable and the same for every op-amp.
The gain is stable: it does not drift with temperature or supply changes (A₀ varies but G does not).
Wider bandwidth (gain × bandwidth ≈ constant) / less distortion / wider linear range of input.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: With negative feedback the gain depends only on resistor values, so it is known and the same for any op-amp; it stays stable when temperature or supply voltage change the open-loop gain; and the amplifier has a much wider bandwidth and less distortion than the op-amp alone.

explanation: Feedback trades gain for predictability, stability and bandwidth.
hints: Think about what happens to A₀ from chip to chip.

stem: A thermocouple probe in a solar geyser gives an output from 0 to $40\ \text{mV}$. Rudo wants a non-inverting amplifier that turns this into 0 to about $4.0\ \text{V}$ for a data logger. The op-amp runs from $\pm 9\ \text{V}$ and has a gain-bandwidth product of $1.0\ \text{MHz}$; $R_1 = 1.0\ \text{k}\Omega$.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the value of R_f needed, in kΩ.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: She uses the standard value $R_f = 100\ \text{k}\Omega$. Calculate the output for an input of $40\ \text{mV}$, in V, to three significant figures.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Explain why a non-inverting amplifier is more suitable here than an inverting one.

points.description: Very high input resistance: it draws almost no current from the thermocouple, so the sensor voltage is not pulled down.
Output is positive (in phase) for a positive input, matching a 0 to 4 V logger input.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The non-inverting amplifier has a very high input resistance, so it draws almost no current from the thermocouple and does not change its voltage, and its output is positive for a positive input, which suits a logger expecting 0 to 4 V.
